channel.title: Audio on Best of AI
channel.description: Recent content in Audio on Best of AI

item.title: Ableton Live
item.description:
It includes instruments, effects, and MIDI tools, plus Max for Live for building custom devices. Newer versions offer stem separation and other assisted features. Live runs on Windows and macOS.

It is sold in several editions at different prices.

Logic Pro and FL Studio are alternatives. Ableton Live suits music producers who perform or work in loops.

item.title: Audacity
item.description:
It records from microphones, edits waveforms, and applies effects such as noise reduction and compression. Plug-ins extend it, and there are AI-based plug-ins for noise and transcription.

It runs on Windows, macOS, and Linux. It is destructive in some workflows, so keep copies of originals.

Adobe Audition and Reaper are alternatives. Audacity suits narrators and podcasters who need a free editor.

item.title: Axon Draft One
item.description:
The system transcribes the recording and produces a first-person narrative in a standard report format. Officers must check facts, correct errors, and attest to the final report. Some agencies add flags that mark AI-drafted text.

It is sold to agencies, and some jurisdictions and prosecutors have set rules on its use.

Transcription tools such as Truleo and Rev serve related needs. Axon Draft One suits police officers who write many reports.

item.title: FL Studio
item.description:
The pattern-based step sequencer and piano roll make it quick to sketch ideas. It comes with synths, samplers, and effects, and includes stem separation. Image-Line has a lifetime free updates policy.

Editions differ by feature set and price.

Ableton Live and Logic Pro are alternatives. FL Studio suits producers who start from beats.

item.title: iZotope Ozone
item.description:
Master Assistant analyzes a track and suggests a starting chain, and users then adjust the modules. It includes a maximizer, imager, and match EQ. Metering shows loudness and spectrum.

Several editions are sold at different prices. Assistant settings are a starting point, not a final master.

LANDR and eMastered offer automated mastering online. Ozone suits sound engineers who master themselves.

item.title: Logic Pro
item.description:
It includes a large library of instruments and loops, plus tools like Session Players, which generate drummer, bass, and keyboard parts. Stem splitter separates tracks from mixed audio. Dolby Atmos mixing is supported.

It is a one-time purchase on Mac and a subscription on iPad.

Ableton Live and FL Studio are alternatives. Logic Pro suits musicians in the Apple ecosystem.

item.title: Pro Tools
item.description:
It handles multitrack recording, comping, and large session management. Surround and Dolby Atmos mixing are supported. It works with Avid and third-party interfaces and plug-ins, and has added assisted features such as stem separation.

It is sold by subscription or perpetual license, with a free entry version.

Logic Pro and Reaper are alternatives. Pro Tools suits sound engineers in professional studios.

item.title: rekordbox
item.description:
It analyzes tracks for beats and key, and sets cue points and playlists. Prepared libraries move to Pioneer DJ players by USB. Newer versions add stem separation and cloud sync.

Basic features are free, and paid plans unlock performance and cloud features.

Serato DJ and Traktor are alternatives. rekordbox suits DJs who play on club standard gear.

item.title: Serato DJ
item.description:
DJs load tracks, loop, set cues, and mix with effects. Stem separation lets them mute vocals or drums in real time. Plans include a free tier for basic use.

Hardware support is wide, though some features need compatible gear.

rekordbox and Traktor are alternatives. Serato DJ suits DJs who want flexible controller support.

item.title: Azure AI Speech
item.description:
Azure AI Speech brings Microsoft’s speech technology into applications. Speech-to-text transcribes audio in real time or from recordings in many languages, with options for custom vocabulary and speaker separation. Text-to-speech offers a large library of neural voices in many languages and styles, with control over tone, speed, and emotion using SSML. Real-time speech translation converts spoken language into another language for captions or voice.

Additional features serve specialized needs. Custom Neural Voice lets approved customers build a branded voice from recorded samples, subject to a restricted-access process to prevent misuse. Voice live and conversational features support building voice agents, and avatar capabilities create talking presenters from text. Container deployments allow running models on premises or at the edge, and the service integrates with Azure OpenAI and other Azure AI tools.

item.title: eMastered
item.description:
eMastered applies automatic mastering to a mixed track. A musician uploads the song, the service analyzes it, and an algorithm processes it for balance, loudness, and clarity so it sounds polished on streaming platforms. Users can adjust settings such as intensity, EQ, and reference tracks before downloading.

It is designed for independent artists and producers who cannot afford a mastering engineer for every release. The process takes minutes and costs less than hiring a professional, and a subscription can cover unlimited masters on some plans.

item.title: Google Cloud Text-to-Speech
item.description:
Google Cloud Text-to-Speech gives developers speech synthesis built on the technology behind Google’s assistants. A request with text returns audio in formats like MP3 or WAV, with a choice of voices and languages. The newer voice families, such as WaveNet and the Chirp generation, sound much more natural than traditional synthetic voices, and there are many accents and genders to choose from.

Developers can fine-tune delivery with SSML, adding pauses, emphasis, pronunciation, and speed. The service supports long audio synthesis for audiobooks and narration, and streaming for real-time applications such as voice assistants and interactive voice response systems. Customers can request a custom voice trained on their own recordings, with strict requirements, and the service integrates with other Google Cloud tools.

item.title: Libsyn
item.description:
Libsyn, short for Liberated Syndication, has hosted podcasts since the early days of the medium. Creators upload audio, and Libsyn produces the RSS feed that podcast apps use, so a show appears across Apple Podcasts, Spotify, and many other directories. It also offers an embeddable player and a basic website.

Pricing has historically been based on the amount of storage you upload each month, which differs from plans tied to downloads. Statistics show downloads by episode and location, and the platform has monetization options, including dynamic ad insertion and sponsorship marketplaces, plus tools for video podcasts and premium subscriptions.

item.title: Superwhisper
item.description:
Superwhisper is a dictation tool. You press a shortcut, speak, and the text appears wherever your cursor is, in an email, a document, or a code editor. Because it can run speech recognition models on your own machine, nothing has to be sent to the cloud, which matters for privacy and works without an internet connection.

Modes make it more than plain transcription. A mode can clean up filler words, format the text as an email or meeting notes, translate it, or follow a custom prompt that uses a language model to rewrite what you said. It also understands context from the app you are in, and supports many languages and voice models, including cloud options for higher accuracy.

item.title: Synthesizer V
item.description:
Synthesizer V is a singing voice synthesizer. A musician enters notes in a piano roll, types lyrics under each note, and the software sings them in a chosen voice. Parameters control pitch, vibrato, breathiness, and timing, so a producer can shape the performance rather than accept a flat robotic output.

The AI voice databases are the main attraction. They are trained on real singers and sound more natural than older concatenative systems, and some support several languages with a single voice. Vocal modes change the style, such as a softer or more intense delivery. Synthesizer V runs as a standalone editor or as a plugin in digital audio workstations, and a free version offers limited features.

item.title: Zencastr
item.description:
Zencastr was built for remote podcast interviews. Instead of recording a call, it captures each participant’s microphone on their own device and uploads the separate tracks, which produces cleaner audio than the compressed stream you hear during a call. Guests join through a link in their browser, with no account needed.

Beyond recording, it offers tools for finishing a show. Automatic post-production levels audio and removes silence, an editor allows basic cuts, and AI features generate transcripts, summaries, and show notes. Video recording and a hosting option cover more of the workflow, and exports go to editing programs.

item.title: Google Genie
item.description: Genie is a different kind of generative model. Instead of producing a fixed image or video, it creates a world you can explore: describe a scene, and the model generates an environment that responds as you move through it, frame by frame, with the scene staying consistent as you turn around. DeepMind frames world models as a step toward AI that understands how environments behave, with possible uses in games, robotics training, and simulation.

item.title: Milan Voice AI
item.description:
Milan Voice AI generates speech for creators and developers. Users type text and choose or create a voice, with options to clone a voice from a short sample or describe a new one. Multi-speaker mode takes a script with several characters and produces a dialogue, useful for podcasts, audiobooks, and videos.

Typical uses include narration, character voices, and prototypes of voice features. An API supports integration into apps. Voice cloning requires permission from the person whose voice is copied, and synthetic audio should be disclosed where appropriate.

item.title: Gemini 3.8 Live
item.description: Google released Gemini 3.8 Live on September 15, 2026, alongside a reasoning-heavier sibling called Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking. Both run over a WebSocket connection through the Gemini Live API, take audio, video, images, and text as input, and reply in audio, understanding and speaking 97 languages with the ability to switch languages mid-conversation. Pricing runs $0.005 per minute of audio input and $0.018 per minute of audio output, which works out to roughly $1.38 for an hour of conversation.

item.title: Whisper
item.description:
Whisper is a speech-to-text model trained on a very large and varied collection of multilingual audio. That training made it unusually robust: it copes with accents, background noise, and technical vocabulary better than many earlier systems, and it works across dozens of languages. It also detects the spoken language automatically, adds punctuation, and can translate speech from other languages into English text.

The model is released as open source with several sizes, from small ones that run on a laptop to large ones that need a good GPU. That openness led to a wide ecosystem: faster versions such as whisper.cpp and faster-whisper, tools that add timestamps and speaker labels, and many apps for transcription, subtitles, and dictation that use it behind the scenes. OpenAI also offers it through its API for people who do not want to host it.

item.title: Amazon Nova Sonic
item.description: Amazon Nova Sonic is a speech-to-speech model that Amazon announced in April 2025, unifying speech understanding and speech generation into a single model rather than chaining separate speech-to-text, language, and text-to-speech systems together. It’s accessed through a bidirectional streaming API on Amazon Bedrock, supports a 300,000-token context window, and is built for real-time voice agents that need to listen, reason, and respond with natural-sounding speech and low latency. It also supports tool use and knowledge grounding, so a voice agent built on Sonic can call external functions or retrieve information mid-conversation.

item.title: AudioCraft
item.description: AudioCraft is a code library that Meta released in August 2023, bundling three generative audio models: MusicGen for text-to-music generation, AudioGen for environmental sound effects, and EnCodec, the neural audio codec both rely on for tokenizing waveforms. MusicGen comes in several sizes (300M, 1.5B, and 3.3B parameters), with variants that can also follow a melody alongside a text prompt, while AudioGen ships as a 1.5B-parameter model trained on sound effects rather than music. Meta released the code and weights under the MIT license, which made AudioCraft one of the first fully open toolkits for text-to-audio generation, in contrast to closed systems from companies like Google. It runs on a single consumer GPU for the smaller checkpoints, and it’s become a common base for open-source music generation projects and research on controllable audio synthesis.

item.title: AudioLM
item.description: AudioLM is a research framework that Google published in September 2022, treating audio generation as a language modeling problem over discrete audio tokens instead of the usual spectrogram or waveform regression approaches. It combines two representations: semantic tokens from w2v-BERT, a self-supervised speech model, that capture long-range structure, and acoustic tokens from the SoundStream neural codec that preserve fine audio detail for high-quality synthesis. Trained only on raw audio with no text transcripts or annotations, it can continue a few seconds of spoken audio or piano music in a way that stays coherent over tens of seconds, something earlier audio generation methods struggled with. Google never released it as a product; it stayed a research paper and demo page, and Google DeepMind used its token-based approach as a building block for later work like MusicLM and parts of Lyria.

item.title: Kimi-Audio
item.description: Kimi-Audio is an open-weight audio foundation model from Moonshot AI, with pretrained and instruction-tuned 7B checkpoints released in late April 2025. It handles speech recognition, audio understanding, and speech generation in a single model, so it can transcribe audio, answer questions about a sound clip, and produce spoken output rather than needing separate models stitched together. Moonshot released the model along with an evaluation toolkit, and the weights and code are on GitHub and Hugging Face under an Apache 2.0 license. It sits alongside Kimi-VL and the Kimi K-series text models in Moonshot’s push to open-source specialized components rather than keep every capability behind a closed API, and it gives developers a free, self-hostable alternative to commercial speech models like OpenAI’s Whisper and Google’s audio models.

item.title: Lyria
item.description: Lyria is Google DeepMind’s music generation model, built to turn text prompts into produced audio tracks. The version available through Vertex AI (Lyria 2) generates instrumental music from text descriptions, handling a wide range of genres and picking up on the texture of individual instruments, while the streaming variant, Lyria RealTime, produces continuous music over a WebSocket connection that responds to live parameter changes. DeepMind pairs every clip with a SynthID watermark so the audio can be identified as AI-generated after the fact.

item.title: Neets AI
item.description:
Neets AI offers speech synthesis through a simple API. Developers send text and choose a voice, and the service returns audio. It emphasizes variety of voices, speed, and low cost, which suits projects that generate large volumes of audio, such as reading articles aloud.

Typical users include app developers, content publishers, and teams building voice agents. Voice quality is good for many purposes, though the top-tier commercial providers may offer more emotion and control. Streaming support makes it usable for interactive applications.

item.title: Soundful
item.description:
Soundful helps creators find music without licensing hassles. A user picks a genre, mood, and tempo, and the platform generates a track that can be customized and downloaded. The pitch is that each track is unique and cleared for use in videos, streams, and podcasts.

It serves YouTubers, streamers, marketers, and podcasters who need background music at scale. Different plans set what usage rights apply, including for monetized content and for commercial work.

item.title: Transistor
item.description:
Transistor is designed for people who run more than one podcast. A single account can host unlimited shows, which suits agencies, companies, and networks, and plans are based on downloads and team size instead of per-show fees. Episodes distribute to Apple Podcasts, Spotify, and other apps through an RSS feed Transistor manages.

Other features address professional needs. Private podcasts let companies share internal or members-only audio, embeddable players and a branded website help promote shows, and detailed analytics show downloads and audience. Collaboration features give team members access to specific shows, and integrations connect with Zapier and other tools. AI tools support transcripts and episode copy.

item.title: The Audio Stuff
item.description:
The Audio Stuff covers personal audio gear with an emphasis on independence. Reviews of headphones, in-ear monitors, speakers, digital-to-analog converters, and amplifiers combine listening impressions with objective measurements, and the site states that it does not publish sponsored reviews. Comparisons and buying guides help readers navigate crowded categories.

For people buying audio equipment, the combination of measured data and subjective notes is useful. Frequency response graphs and other measurements show how products behave, which helps predict how they will sound, and the writing explains what that means for different music and preferences. The site also covers news and recommendations for budgets.

item.title: Adobe Enhance Speech
item.description: Enhance Speech is a simple tool with a dramatic effect. You upload a recording of a voice, such as an interview, podcast, voiceover, or video narration, and the AI processes it to remove noise, reverb, and room echo, and rebalances the voice. In moments, a recording made on a phone in a kitchen can sound much closer to something recorded in a studio. It has become popular among creators who record in imperfect spaces.

item.title: Adobe Podcast
item.description:
Adobe Podcast started with one very useful trick: you upload a voice recording made in a noisy room, and it comes back sounding like it was recorded in a studio. Enhance Speech removes hiss, echo, and background noise and evens out the voice. People use it to rescue interview audio, remote recordings, and phone-quality clips, and it works well on single speakers talking clearly.

The wider product is a browser-based recording and editing studio. You can record yourself or a remote guest, then edit by deleting words in the transcript, much like editing a text document. Features that clean up speech, adjust volume, and add music or sound effects sit alongside it. A mic check tool tests how your setup sounds before you start. Because everything runs in the browser, there is nothing to install, and files can be exported for use in other editors.

item.title: AIVA
item.description: AIVA, short for Artificial Intelligence Virtual Artist, was built to compose music, with an early emphasis on classical and cinematic styles. You pick a style from a library of hundreds, set the length and key, and it generates a track. You can also upload an audio or MIDI file as an influence, or define your own chord progression. Video creators, game developers, podcasters, and advertisers use it to get background music without hiring a composer.

item.title: Altered AI
item.description:
Altered focuses on voice conversion, sometimes called speech-to-speech. You record a performance, and the system re-voices it in another voice from its library while keeping the timing, emotion, and delivery of the original. That differs from text-to-speech, where the machine invents the performance. For productions, it means one actor can voice several characters, or a performance can be changed to match a different character without a second recording session.

The tools are designed for professionals. Altered Studio provides a way to process recordings and fine-tune results, and the platform includes text-to-speech and voice cloning options for productions that need them. Typical customers are game studios, audiobook makers, animation and film teams, and agencies that localize content. Licensed voices matter in this field, since using someone’s voice without permission raises legal and ethical issues.

item.title: Auphonic
item.description:
Auphonic automates the finishing steps of audio production. You upload a recording, such as a podcast episode or interview, and it applies adaptive leveling to even out volume differences between speakers, normalizes loudness to the standards used by streaming and broadcast, reduces background noise and hum, and applies filtering to improve clarity. The result is consistent, professional sounding audio with little manual work.

It supports multitrack recordings, where each person is recorded separately, and balances them automatically. Additional features include speech recognition to create transcripts, chapter marks, and exports to podcast hosts and cloud storage, and an API allows batch processing. Presets and a web interface make it approachable for non-engineers, and it’s used by independent podcasters, radio stations, and educators.

item.title: Beatoven.ai
item.description: Beatoven.ai is aimed at video makers, podcasters, and game developers who need background music without searching a stock library. You describe the track you want, such as a calm acoustic piece for a travel vlog, or choose a genre, mood, and duration, and the AI composes an original piece. You can change the emotion of different sections along the timeline, which is helpful when a video moves from a tense moment to a resolved one.

item.title: Boomy
item.description: Boomy is one of the easiest ways to generate music. You pick a style such as lo-fi, electronic, rap beats, or cinematic, and the system composes a track in moments. You can then adjust it by changing the arrangement, adding vocals or effects, and recording your own voice over the music. It requires no musical knowledge, which is why it appeals to casual creators and people who want custom background tracks.

item.title: Buzzsprout
item.description:
Buzzsprout focuses on being the easiest way to get a podcast online. You upload an audio file, add show notes, and publish, and it distributes the episode to Apple Podcasts, Spotify, and other directories through an RSS feed it manages. It provides an embeddable player for your website, detailed download statistics, and tools for promoting episodes on social media.

Additional features help creators improve and grow. Magic Mastering automatically cleans up and balances audio loudness, an AI transcription service creates transcripts, and tools can generate chapters, episode titles, and descriptions. Dynamic content features and a way to import an existing podcast make switching easy. Monetization options include support from listeners and ads in some plans.

item.title: Cartesia
item.description:
Cartesia focuses on speed in voice AI. Its Sonic models, built on state-space model architectures instead of only transformers, generate natural-sounding speech with very low latency, so a voice agent can start speaking almost as soon as a response is ready. That matters for phone calls and live assistants, where delays feel awkward. The company also offers voice cloning and control over emotion and speaking rate.

The platform has grown into a set of real-time voice building blocks. Sonic handles text-to-speech, Ink handles speech-to-text, and tools for managed voice agents help companies deploy agents that answer phone calls. Developers connect through APIs and SDKs, and Cartesia works with common voice agent frameworks and telephony providers. Multilingual support lets one system serve customers in different languages.

item.title: Cleanfeed
item.description:
Cleanfeed lets people record or broadcast audio over the internet without installing software. A host creates a session, guests join by link in a browser, and the platform streams audio with low delay and records each participant on a separate track. It is popular with radio and podcast teams who need dependable quality.

The audio chain is a focus. It offers a noise gate, level controls, and processing options that tidy up voices, plus connections for studio equipment and phone callers. Producers can monitor and route audio, record backups, and download multitrack files. A newer version improves collaboration and integration with video.

item.title: Cleanvoice
item.description: Cleanvoice does one job: it cleans up speech. You upload a podcast episode, interview, or video, and it finds the places where a speaker said “um” or “uh,” paused for too long, made lip smacks or breath sounds, or repeated a word. It removes them and returns a tidier file. Editing these by hand takes a long time, and a one-hour recording can contain hundreds of them, so automating it saves real hours for podcasters and video creators.

item.title: Descript
item.description:
Descript changed podcast editing by turning audio into text. After you record or import an episode, it transcribes it, and you cut, move, and delete sections by editing the words, which is much faster than working on waveforms. Filler words and long pauses can be removed in bulk, and multitrack editing, music, and effects are available for more polished shows.

Recording and polishing tools are built in. Remote recording captures guests in high quality, Studio Sound improves voice clarity and reduces noise, and an Overdub feature can fix mistakes with a synthetic version of your voice. AI assistants draft titles, descriptions, and show notes, suggest chapters, and generate clips and audiograms for social media. Episodes can be published to hosting platforms or exported.

item.title: Descript
item.description: Descript changed how many people edit audio and video. You upload a recording, it produces a transcript, and you cut, rearrange, and delete the media by editing the text like a document. Removing a sentence in the transcript removes it from the recording. For podcasts, interviews, tutorials, and talking-head videos, that is much faster than working on a waveform, and people who have never used an editor can pick it up quickly.

item.title: Descript Studio Sound
item.description:
Studio Sound targets the common problem of recording in imperfect spaces. Apply it to a clip in Descript, and the AI removes noise, reduces echo and reverb, and evens out the voice, making recordings made on a laptop or phone sound much more professional. It works on a whole project or a selected portion and has an intensity setting, so you can balance cleanup against natural sound.

It is built into Descript’s editing workflow, so you can clean audio while editing the transcript, and it works on both audio and video projects. Podcasters, interviewers, educators, and video creators use it to rescue recordings from noisy environments. It can be combined with other features in Descript, such as filler word removal and eye contact correction for video.

item.title: Dolby.io
item.description:
Dolby.io brings Dolby’s audio expertise to developers as web services. A developer sends an audio or video file and receives a processed version: cleaner speech, reduced background noise, balanced loudness, or improved dialogue. These APIs fit podcast tools, video platforms, and conferencing products.

Other parts of the platform focus on real-time streaming. Millicast delivers low-latency video to large audiences, which suits live events, interactive broadcasts, and remote production. Analysis and transcoding APIs help prepare content for different devices.

item.title: ElevenLabs
item.description:
ElevenLabs is known for natural-sounding synthetic speech. Users type text and choose a voice, or clone a voice from a sample, and get audio that carries intonation and emotion. The platform supports dozens of languages and accents and offers a library of voices.

Its products now span several uses. Dubbing translates video into other languages while keeping the speaker’s voice, audiobook and narration tools produce long-form audio, and a conversational agent platform builds voice assistants that talk with customers in real time. Music and sound effect generation, plus speech to text, round out the suite. An API lets developers embed these features.

item.title: ElevenLabs
item.description: ElevenLabs is best known for text-to-speech that sounds like a person rather than a robot. You paste in a script, choose a voice from a large library or make your own, and the tool reads it with natural pacing and emotion. The same voice can speak dozens of languages, which makes it a popular option for audiobooks, YouTube narration, e-learning, game characters, and accessibility. Voice cloning builds a copy of a voice from a recording, and there are safeguards around it: you are meant to have the speaker’s permission, and some features require identity checks.

item.title: ElevenLabs Sound Effects
item.description:
ElevenLabs Sound Effects creates audio from a sentence. You describe the sound you need, such as a door creaking in an empty house or a crowd cheering in a stadium, and the model generates several options in seconds, which you can adjust for length and download. This helps video editors, game developers, podcasters, and filmmakers who otherwise search libraries for the right clip or record effects themselves.

The company also offers a Voice Isolator that separates speech from background noise and music, helping clean up interviews and field recordings. These tools fit alongside ElevenLabs’ text-to-speech, dubbing, and music features, so a creator can produce a full soundtrack in one place. An API allows developers to generate effects inside apps and games.

item.title: Hume AI
item.description: Hume AI started from research on human emotion. Its models analyze the way people speak and show emotion, including tone, pace, and inflection, and its Empathic Voice Interface (EVI) uses that understanding in a conversational voice assistant. EVI listens to the user’s voice, picks up on cues like frustration or excitement, and adjusts its responses and speaking style accordingly, so a voice agent can feel more natural than one that only transcribes words.

item.title: iZotope RX
item.description:
RX is the tool engineers reach for when audio is flawed. Its spectral display shows sound as an image, making it possible to see and remove specific problems, such as a cough, a phone buzz, or a chair squeak, without affecting the rest. Modules cover denoising, de-clicking, de-hum, de-reverb, de-clipping, and other repair tasks, and are used by post-production teams, podcast producers, forensic analysts, and musicians.

Machine learning powers its newer tools. Dialogue Isolate separates speech from background sounds, Music Rebalance lets you adjust the levels of vocals, bass, and drums in a finished mix, and Spectral Recovery restores high frequencies lost in low-quality files. Dialogue Contour and other features help produce consistent speech. It works as a standalone editor and as plugins in digital audio workstations and video editors.

item.title: Krisp
item.description: Krisp installs as a virtual microphone and speaker, so it sits between your hardware and whatever calling app you use. It removes noise before it reaches the other person: barking dogs, keyboard clatter, traffic, and other voices in the room. It can also clean incoming audio, so a participant on a bad connection or in a loud space sounds clearer to you. Because it works with Zoom, Teams, Meet, Slack, and nearly any other app, one setup covers all of them.

item.title: LANDR
item.description:
LANDR started with automated mastering. An artist uploads a mixed song, the system analyzes it, and an algorithm applies equalization, compression, and loudness adjustments, producing a master in minutes at a price below hiring an engineer. Style and loudness options guide the result.

The company now offers a wider set of services for independent musicians: distribution to streaming platforms, a marketplace of samples, plugins, a collaboration network, and tools for mixing and creating. A subscription bundles many of these.

item.title: Loudly
item.description:
Loudly offers music for people who need soundtracks without composing. Users can create tracks by choosing a genre, mood, and tempo, or by describing what they want in a prompt, and then download the result. A library of ready-made AI tracks lets you browse by genre and use case. It is intended for video creators, podcasters, streamers, game developers, and businesses that need background music.

Several features support practical use. A personalization option adjusts elements like instruments and structure, stems can be downloaded for editing, and an API allows developers to embed music generation in their own products, such as apps that need adaptive soundtracks. The company positions its music as safe for commercial use, with licenses that cover content on social platforms.

item.title: Lovo AI
item.description:
Lovo makes synthetic speech for creators and businesses. Users type or paste a script, choose a voice, and adjust tone, speed, and emphasis to generate narration. Genny, the editor, lets them place speech alongside video, images, and music in one timeline.

Voice cloning and a marketplace of voices expand the options, and the platform supports many languages. Typical uses are explainer videos, e-learning, ads, and audiobooks. An API provides access for developers.

item.title: Murf
item.description: Murf is known for its studio, but its voice features are a separate reason people use it. The voice changer converts a recording of your own speech into a different voice from the library, keeping your timing and emotion, which suits people who want a polished sound without hiring talent. Voice cloning can create a custom voice for a brand or presenter, typically with consent and verification, and is offered mainly for business customers.

item.title: Murf
item.description:
Murf is aimed at people who need a professional voiceover without hiring a voice actor or booking a studio. In its browser-based studio, you paste a script, choose a voice, and adjust pitch, speed, and emphasis. Voices come in many accents and languages and suit narration, e-learning, product videos, ads, and presentations. You can add background music, line the audio up with video or slides, and export the result.

The platform has expanded to related audio jobs. Dubbing translates a video or audio file into other languages and keeps it timed to the original. An API gives developers text-to-speech for their own apps, including fast, streaming voices for conversational use. Murf Agents power voice calls and chat for customer service and similar needs, and a voice changer converts one voice into another. Team workspaces help companies share projects and keep audio consistent.

item.title: Notta
item.description: Notta turns speech into text for people who sit through many conversations. You can record in the mobile or web app, upload audio and video files, or let its assistant join Zoom, Google Meet, and Teams calls. The transcript appears in the app with speaker labels and timestamps, and you can search it, edit it, and share it. It supports a large number of languages, which suits international teams, journalists, and researchers.

item.title: Replica Studios
item.description:
Replica Studios was an Australian startup that made AI voices aimed at creative productions. Its library offered voices of professional actors who had agreed to license their performances, and its tools let game developers and filmmakers generate dialogue with emotion and style. Integrations for game engines such as Unreal and Unity made it easy to put placeholder or final voices into a project, and it also supported voice conversion.

The company drew attention for working with actors instead of against them. It signed an agreement with the actors’ union SAG-AFTRA on terms for licensing digital voice replicas in games, which some actors welcomed and others criticized as inadequate. That debate was part of a wider fight over how AI voices should be used in entertainment, which continues.

item.title: Resemble AI
item.description: Resemble AI builds voices for products and productions. You provide recordings of a speaker, with consent, and the platform trains a voice model that can read any text in that voice, or convert one person’s speech into another voice in real time. Companies use it for branded voices, localization, games, call centers, and media. An API makes it possible to generate speech in applications, and the system supports multiple languages and emotional control.

item.title: Riverside
item.description: Riverside solves a familiar remote-recording problem: video calls compress audio and video, so the recording sounds and looks poor. Riverside records each person’s microphone and camera on their own device and uploads the files in the background. The result is uncompressed audio and up to 4K video, with each participant on a separate track, unaffected by a weak internet connection during the call. Hosts and guests join through a browser link without installing anything.

item.title: Sonix
item.description:
Sonix focuses on fast, accurate machine transcription with a polished editor. You upload a file or connect a source, and get a transcript with timestamps and speaker labels, which you can edit while listening and the text highlights as the audio plays. It supports over forty languages and can translate transcripts into many more. Journalists, researchers, podcasters, and video producers use it to turn recordings into searchable text.

Additional tools support publishing. Sonix exports subtitles and captions in standard formats, offers a media player that embeds the transcript, and provides search across all your files. Integrations and an API connect it with video editors like Premiere Pro and Final Cut, and Zoom. Teams can share folders and custom vocabulary to improve accuracy on specialized terms.

item.title: Speechify
item.description: Speechify turns reading into listening. You import text from the web, a PDF, an email, or a photo of a page, and the app reads it aloud at the speed you choose, highlighting the words as it goes. That makes it useful for catching up on articles while commuting, for studying, and for people with dyslexia or other reading differences, who often find audio easier to process. Apps for iOS, Android, Chrome, and the web sync your library.

item.title: Spotify for Podcasters
item.description:
Spotify for Podcasters grew from Anchor, an app that made podcasting free and easy. Creators can record from a phone or computer, upload episodes, and publish to Spotify, Apple Podcasts, and other directories from one place, with no hosting fees. Tools include simple editing, music and sound effects, and a way to bring in guests remotely.

The creator tools have expanded to include video podcasts, which Spotify has promoted heavily, along with analytics on audience size, demographics, and listening behavior. Monetization options include ad insertion, listener subscriptions, and partner programs for eligible shows. The brand has been folded into Spotify for Creators, which covers audio and video content creators on the platform.

item.title: Voicemod
item.description: Voicemod changes how you sound as you speak. You choose a voice effect, such as a robot, a deep voice, or a character, and the app processes your microphone audio in real time. It works as a virtual microphone, so apps like Discord, Zoom, OBS, and many games treat it like a normal mic. Gamers and streamers use it for fun and for roleplay, and some people use it for privacy.

item.title: WellSaid Labs
item.description:
WellSaid focuses on voiceovers for businesses. In its web studio, you type or paste a script, pick a voice, and generate narration with control over pacing, pronunciation, and emphasis. The voices are built from recordings by professional voice actors who agreed to the use, which gives companies a clear license position. Typical projects include training courses, explainer videos, product tours, corporate announcements, and audio for apps.

For larger teams, collaboration and control matter. Projects can be shared, commented on, and reviewed, and custom pronunciation settings keep brand names and technical terms consistent across a library of content. An API lets developers add speech to their own products, and integrations connect WellSaid to e-learning and creative tools. Enterprise plans emphasize security, privacy, and compliance, and custom voices can be created for a brand.

item.title: ACE Studio
item.description: ACE Studio lets musicians create vocals without a singer. You enter a melody in a piano-roll editor along with lyrics, choose a voice model, and the software sings it, with controls for vibrato, breath, dynamics, and expression that make the performance sound human. It works as a standalone app or as a plugin inside digital audio workstations such as Ableton, Logic, and FL Studio. Songwriters use it for demos and finished tracks.

item.title: Fish Audio
item.description:
Fish Audio generates synthetic speech with an emphasis on voice variety. Users type text, choose a voice, and get audio. A cloning feature creates a voice from a short sample, and a public library offers voices shared by other users, including character and celebrity-style options.

Creators use it for narration, videos, games, and podcasts, and developers integrate it through an API for apps and agents. The company has released open models for speech synthesis, which has helped it build a community of users and researchers.

item.title: Gladia
item.description:
Gladia provides speech-to-text as a service for developers. Companies send audio from calls, meetings, or videos and receive transcripts with timestamps, speaker labels, and optional translation. It handles dozens of languages and can detect which one is being spoken.

Real-time transcription suits live captioning and voice agents, while batch processing handles recordings at scale. Extra features include summaries, sentiment, and named entity detection. The API is aimed at products built on audio, such as meeting assistants, call analytics, and media tools.

item.title: Jammable
item.description:
Jammable, formerly Voicify, lets people hear songs sung in a different voice. A user chooses a voice model from a library, uploads a vocal or song, and the system converts it so it sounds like the chosen voice. Fans and creators use it for parodies, mashups, and experiments.

The technology raises serious legal and ethical issues. Voices of real artists are protected in many places, and music labels and artists have objected to unauthorized voice clones. Sharing such covers can violate copyright and rights of publicity, and platforms may remove them. Use voices you have permission to use, and avoid presenting synthetic songs as the real artist.

item.title: Kits AI
item.description:
Kits AI targets music creators. A producer can record a vocal and convert it into another singer’s voice from a library, create a model of their own voice for consistent takes, or separate a song into vocals and instruments to remix. A text to speech option and tools for vocal cleanup are included.

Its distinguishing approach is licensing. Kits offers voices from artists who have agreed to participate and be paid, which contrasts with unauthorized voice clones that raise copyright and rights-of-publicity problems. Users still need to follow license terms for how converted vocals are released.

item.title: Moises
item.description:
Moises helps musicians work with recordings. A user uploads a song, and the app splits it into individual tracks, so a guitarist can mute the guitar and play along, or a singer can remove the lead vocal for practice. Tempo and key changes help with learning difficult parts.

Extra tools include chord detection, a metronome, and a feature to detect beats. Producers use stem separation for remixes and sampling, and teachers use it to demonstrate parts. Mobile and web apps make it easy to practice anywhere.

item.title: Musicfy
item.description:
Musicfy offers several music tools in one place. Users can generate a track from a text prompt, convert one instrument or vocal to another voice or sound, separate a song into stems, and create voice covers with AI voices. It is aimed at creators who want to experiment with songs without a studio.

The same tools raise rights questions. Copying a real artist’s voice without permission can violate publicity and copyright rules, and platforms and labels remove such content. Generated music has varying licensing terms, so read them before releasing or monetizing songs.

item.title: Podcastle
item.description:
Podcastle is a browser-based studio for audio. Users can record remote interviews with separate tracks, edit by working with the transcript, and clean up audio with one-click enhancement that removes noise and levels voices. A text-to-speech and voice cloning feature lets creators fix a mistake by typing.

The platform includes tools for video podcasts, hosting and distribution, and AI features such as summaries and show notes. It aims to give new podcasters an all-in-one workflow without learning a traditional audio editor.

item.title: Respeecher
item.description:
Respeecher works through speech-to-speech conversion. A performer records a line, and the system transforms it into the voice of a target speaker, keeping the performer’s emotion and timing. This differs from text-to-speech, which generates speech from scratch and can lack nuance.

Productions have used it to recreate the voices of actors who are unavailable, age or de-age a voice, and dub into other languages while preserving a character’s sound. The company emphasizes licensing and consent from voice owners.

item.title: Riffusion
item.description:
Riffusion started as a research demo that generated music clips by running Stable Diffusion on spectrogram images, an early sign that diffusion models could make audio. It grew into a platform where users type a prompt and get a song with vocals, and into a chat-like agent that helps produce tracks.

The brand changed to Producer.ai, and reports say it has since moved under Google’s music efforts, so product names and features may keep changing. Users should check the current site and how their saved songs and rights are handled through any transition.

item.title: Speechmatics
item.description:
Speechmatics provides speech-to-text as a service. Developers send audio and get transcripts with timestamps, speaker labels, and language detection. The company emphasizes accuracy across accents and dialects, which is an area where many systems show bias.

Products include real-time transcription for live captioning and voice agents, batch processing, translation, and deployment options on premises for sensitive data. Customers include media, contact center, and healthcare companies.

Speechmatics is priced by usage. Alternatives include Deepgram, AssemblyAI, OpenAI Whisper, Gladia, and Google Cloud Speech-to-Text. Speechmatics suits organizations needing accurate multilingual transcription.

item.title: Splice
item.description:
Splice supplies the building blocks of modern production. Producers search a huge catalog of samples by genre, key, and tempo, preview them in sync with their project, and download them under a license that allows use in released music. Plugin subscriptions let users rent instruments and effects.

AI features assist with creativity. Tools suggest compatible samples, and apps generate loops and ideas. Cloud project backup and collaboration features help producers work with others.

item.title: Stable Audio
item.description:
Stable Audio generates sound from descriptions. A user types a prompt such as an upbeat electronic track with a driving bass line, and the model produces a piece of the requested length. It can also create sound effects and ambient textures.

The models were trained on licensed audio, which Stability emphasizes to address rights concerns. Producers and sound designers use it for sketching ideas, backing tracks, and game audio. Smaller open models can run locally.

item.title: Transkriptor
item.description:
Transkriptor turns speech into text. Users upload files, record in the app, or connect meeting platforms, and receive a transcript with timestamps and speaker labels that can be edited and exported. Subtitles and translations are supported.

Features include meeting bots that join calls, AI summaries, and a chat assistant to ask questions about a recording. It serves students, journalists, researchers, and businesses.

Transkriptor has a free trial and paid plans by hours. Accuracy depends on audio quality, and sensitive recordings need privacy checks. Alternatives include Otter.ai, Trint, Descript, Fireflies, and Whisper-based tools. Transkriptor suits people transcribing interviews and meetings.

item.title: Trint
item.description:
Trint speeds up working with recordings. Users upload interviews, press conferences, or footage and get transcripts that link to the audio, so editing the text is easy to verify. Teams can search across an archive, highlight quotes, and build stories from selections.

The platform supports many languages, translation, and subtitles, and offers collaboration for newsrooms with permissions and shared workspaces. AI features create summaries and help extract key moments.

Trint is paid, with plans by features and seats. Accuracy depends on audio quality. Alternatives include Otter.ai, Descript, Transkriptor, Verbit, and Rev. Trint suits media teams that work with large volumes of recorded content.

item.title: Verbit
item.description:
Verbit blends machine and human work. AI produces a first draft of the transcript, and professional editors review and correct it, which yields higher accuracy than automatic transcription alone. Services include captioning for live events, court reporting, and transcripts of recorded media.

Education is a big market: universities use Verbit to caption lectures and meet accessibility requirements. Its platform integrates with video tools and learning systems, and the company has acquired several transcription and captioning firms.

item.title: Amazon Polly
item.description:
Polly takes text and returns audio, which developers call from their apps to add speech. It offers dozens of voices across many languages and accents, built on several engines. The neural voices sound considerably more natural than the older standard ones, and newer generative voices push realism further. It is used for reading articles aloud, voicing phone systems and assistants, creating e-learning narration, and adding accessibility features to apps.

Control over how things are said is a strength. SSML tags let you adjust pauses, emphasis, pitch, speed, and the way numbers, dates, and abbreviations are spoken. Custom lexicons teach Polly the right pronunciation of brand names and jargon. It can also return speech marks that tell your app when each word is spoken, which is useful for highlighting text in sync with audio. Output can be streamed or saved as files in common formats.

item.title: AssemblyAI
item.description:
AssemblyAI is infrastructure for apps that need to understand speech. A developer sends audio from a call, meeting, podcast, or video, and the API returns an accurate transcript with word-level timestamps. It supports pre-recorded files and real-time streaming, so it can power live captions and voice assistants as well as batch transcription. Customers use it to build call analytics, meeting note takers, media search, and compliance tools.

Beyond transcription, a layer of speech understanding turns text into structured data. It can separate speakers, summarize a conversation, detect topics, and score sentiment. Guardrails features redact personal information and filter sensitive content before the data goes anywhere else. An LLM Gateway lets developers pass transcripts to language models for tasks like extracting action items, and a voice agent API supports speech-to-speech applications.

item.title: Deepgram
item.description:
Deepgram sells speech AI to developers. Its speech-to-text API transcribes audio in real time or from recordings, and it is designed for accuracy at low latency and low cost, which matters for call centers, meeting tools, and voice assistants that process large volumes. Features include speaker labeling, punctuation, keyword boosting, and support for many languages, and models can be customized to a company’s vocabulary.

The platform has widened to cover the whole voice stack. A text-to-speech product generates natural voices with low latency, and a voice agent API combines speech recognition, a language model, and speech synthesis into a single service for building conversational agents that can hold phone calls. Enterprises can run Deepgram in their own cloud or on-premises when data cannot leave their control.

item.title: EchoWrite
item.description:
EchoWrite aims to make dictation work everywhere on a Windows PC. A user presses a hotkey, speaks, and the text appears in the active application, such as a word processor, email client, or code editor. AI cleans up punctuation and filler words so the result reads closer to written text.

Voice typing is faster than typing for many people, and helps those with repetitive strain issues. Accuracy depends on the microphone, accent, and vocabulary, and a quiet environment helps. Specialized terms may need custom dictionaries.

item.title: Kokoro TTS
item.description:
Kokoro is notable for doing a lot with a little. The model is small enough to run on a laptop, a phone, or a modest server, yet produces speech that many listeners find clear and natural in several voices. That makes it practical for local and low-cost deployments.

Developers use it for narration, accessibility tools, voice agents, and offline applications, and community projects have packaged it for the browser and for popular frameworks. The license is permissive, which allows commercial use, and the weights are available on Hugging Face.

item.title: Mubert
item.description:
Mubert generates music in real time. You pick a mood, genre, or activity, such as focus, workout, or sleep, and it streams a continuous track that does not loop in an obvious way. Creators use it for background music in videos, streams, podcasts, and apps, and the royalty-free licensing makes it practical for online content.

Several products serve different needs. Mubert Render lets users create tracks of a chosen length from a text prompt or style, and a mobile app offers streaming for listening. An API allows developers to add generated music to games, fitness apps, and other products, delivering music that adapts to context. Artists can contribute sounds to the system, with revenue sharing for contributors.

item.title: PlayHT
item.description: PlayHT offered realistic text-to-speech with a large catalog of voices across many languages, plus voice cloning from short audio samples. Creators used its web studio to narrate videos, podcasts, and audiobooks, and developers used its API to add speech to apps and phone systems. Its later conversational models were built to sound natural in dialogue, with emotion and pacing, and the company also developed voice agents under the PlayAI name.

item.title: Soundraw
item.description:
Soundraw makes custom background music for creators. You select parameters such as mood, genre, theme, tempo, and length, and the AI generates a number of options. You can then adjust the track in an editor, changing the intensity of different sections and instruments to match the pacing of a video, and download the result. This is more flexible than browsing a fixed stock library.

It’s aimed at content creators, marketers, filmmakers, and developers who need affordable music. The subscription offers unlimited downloads and a license for use on social platforms and in commercial projects, with protections against copyright claims on the creator’s own content. The tracks are made from music produced by in-house artists, and Soundraw positions the training data as licensed.

item.title: Suno
item.description: Suno made AI music accessible. You describe the song you want, such as an upbeat pop track about a road trip, or paste your own lyrics, and Suno produces complete songs with singing and instrumentation in under a minute. Users can choose styles and genres, extend and edit songs, create covers, and make instrumentals. It has been used for demos, background music, parody, and just for fun by people with no musical training.

item.title: Udio
item.description:
Udio produces music with an emphasis on audio quality and handling of lyrics. You describe a song or supply lyrics, and Udio generates clips that you can extend into full tracks, remix, and edit section by section. Users liked it for realistic vocals and for the control it gives over structure, and it has been used for songwriting ideas, demos, and entertainment.

Its path changed after legal disputes with major record labels. Udio reached licensing agreements with some labels and moved toward a platform where creation and sharing happen inside the service, often described as a walled garden, with limits on downloading tracks. Plans to build tools around licensed music mean terms can continue to change, and the experience differs from earlier versions, which let users download freely.

item.title: Voicetype AI
item.description:
Voicetype AI lets people speak instead of type. A user holds a hotkey, speaks, and the text appears in the active app, with punctuation and formatting handled automatically. It works across email, documents, chat, and code editors.

AI cleans up filler words and false starts, and supports many languages. Custom dictionaries help with names and jargon. Dictation can speed up writing for people who think out loud.

Voicetype AI has a free tier and paid plans. Independent information is limited, so check privacy and where audio is processed. Alternatives include Wispr Flow, Superwhisper, Dragon, Apple dictation, and Talon. Voicetype AI suits people who want voice typing everywhere.
